posts.title: The Lighthouse Was Gone at Dawn

images.alt: The old and new Scotch Cap lighthouses on Unimak Island before the concrete lighthouse was destroyed by the April 1, 1946 tsunami.
Chief Boatswain’s Mate Anthony L. Petit, officer in charge of Scotch Cap Lighthouse when the 1946 tsunami killed its five-man crew.
Broken concrete and debris where Scotch Cap Lighthouse stood after the April 1, 1946 tsunami.
Aerial photograph of the destroyed Scotch Cap light station on Unimak Island after the 1946 tsunami.
Tsunami water inundating the Hilo waterfront in April 1946, with a person visible near the advancing water.
Debris covering a Hilo street and partly burying a vehicle after the April 1, 1946 tsunami.

posts.title: The Cell Was Built to Hold a Man

images.alt: Stone prison cell in Saint-Pierre associated with survivor Louis-Auguste Cyparis after the 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée.
Saint-Pierre and its roadstead before the 1902 eruption, with Mount Pelée rising beyond the city.
Busy commercial waterfront at Saint-Pierre before the 1902 eruption of Mount Pelee.
An early morning eruption of Mount Pelée photographed in 1902, with a dense volcanic cloud rising from the mountain.
Ruins of Saint-Pierre after the 1902 eruption, looking north toward Mount Pelée in the distance.
Panoramic view across destroyed Saint-Pierre and its bay after the May 1902 Mount Pelée eruption.
A house partly submerged in Hebgen Lake beside a broken roadway after the 1959 earthquake.
Fresh fault scarp near Hebgen Lake produced by the August 1959 earthquake.
The Madison Slide and rapidly filling Earthquake Lake four days after the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake, with camping gear abandoned by survivors in the foreground.
Dragline excavating the Earthquake Lake spillway on October 18, 1959, with one of the nighttime lighting plants visible on the hillside.
Rockslide damage along the Golden Gate road near Mammoth Hot Springs caused by the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake.
Sapphire Pool in Yellowstone erupting after the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake altered the park’s hydrothermal system.
Seismic Geyser erupting in Yellowstone in 1970 after developing from a fracture formed following the 1959 earthquake.
Earthquake Lake in 2023 with standing dead trees in the water and the 1959 Madison Slide scar visible beyond the lake.

posts.title: The Lines Were in the Fire

images.alt: Aerial view of Pearl Harbor's West Loch on May 21, 1944, showing burning LSTs at berths T-8 and T-9 while other landing ships maneuver away.
U.S. Marines wading ashore from USS LST-353 at Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville, on November 6, 1943.
Smoke rising from the wreck of USS LST-480 as tugs and other craft fight fires in West Loch, with burning USS LST-39 at left.
Burned-out USS LST-39 grounded near the Pearl Harbor Naval Ammunition Depot on May 22, 1944.
Firefighters working aboard a destroyed landing ship in West Loch on the morning after the 1944 explosions.
The wreck of USS LST-480 burning again in West Loch on May 23, 1944, with the sunken remains of LST-353 nearby.
Overhead view of the burning hulk of USS LST-480 in West Loch, Pearl Harbor, on May 22, 1944.
Headstone marking two unidentified West Loch disaster victims.
The recovered Palomares nuclear weapon aboard USS Petrel after its recovery from the Mediterranean in April 1966.
Map of the eastern Operation Chrome Dome airborne-alert route showing refueling tracks near Spain.
USS Skill operating off Spain in February 1966 as part of the Palomares search task force.
The submersible Alvin being lowered into the Mediterranean during the 1966 search for the missing Palomares nuclear weapon.
CURV I remotely operated recovery vehicle aboard USS Petrel during the Palomares operation.
Carl Brashear preparing to dive from USS Hunley in 1971 after returning to Navy diving with an artificial leg.
U.S. Navy personnel aboard USS Petrel after recovery of the Palomares hydrogen bomb, with CURV visible in the background.
Barrels of contaminated soil collected at Palomares in 1966 for shipment to the United States.
The damaged Mark 28 nuclear weapon recovered from the Mediterranean and displayed aboard USS Petrel after the Palomares search.

posts.title: The Filter Was at the Top

images.alt: Windscale Pile 1 and Pile 2 in 1951 with their distinctive filter galleries mounted at the tops of the ventilation chimneys.
The Windscale Piles under construction in the late 1940s, showing the massive reactor and chimney structures taking shape.
The Pile Fuel Storage Pond at Sellafield, which received irradiated fuel from the Windscale Piles and fuel removed during the 1957 fire response.
The filter gallery under construction at the top of a Windscale chimney during the late 1940s or early 1950s.
The Windscale Pile 1 chimney diffuser and filter-gallery structure before dismantling.
Sellafield decommissioning workers cutting concrete blocks from the top of the Windscale Pile 1 chimney.
SPIDA suspended hydraulic work platform being lifted into place on a replica chimney during off-site testing for Windscale Pile 1 demolition.
Windscale Pile 1 at Sellafield in 2025 after removal of the filter gallery and diffuser, with the remaining chimney barrel standing beside the reactor building.
The preserved 1628 warship Vasa inside the Vasa Museum in Stockholm, showing the tall upperworks above the hull.
Painted one-tenth-scale reconstruction of Vasa showing how the heavily armed warship likely appeared in 1628.
Full-scale reconstruction of Vasa's upper gun deck showing cannon positions and the confined deck space.
Original 24-pound bronze cannon from Vasa displayed at the Vasa Museum.
Vasa Museum model showing Vasa heeling as water enters the open lower gunports during the 1628 sinking.
Forensic facial reconstructions based on human remains recovered from Vasa and displayed at the Vasa Museum.
Vasa breaking the water surface during the salvage operation at 9:03 a.m. on April 24, 1961.
Vasa inside the museum with old and new support structures used to reduce continuing deformation of the historic hull.
A U.S. Coast Guard helicopter hovering beside the fire-damaged cruise ship Prinsendam during the October 1980 rescue.
Prinsendam at Rotterdam's Wilhelminakade in 1973, seven years before the Gulf of Alaska fire.
Passenger ship Prinsendam during her launch at a Dutch shipyard.
A U.S. Coast Guard HH-3F helicopter operating near the damaged Prinsendam in the Gulf of Alaska in 1980.
Prinsendam listing heavily in the Gulf of Alaska after the 1980 fire and evacuation.
Historical illustration of the Coast Guard rescue operation around Prinsendam in the Gulf of Alaska.
A rapidly enlarging breach reaching the crest of Teton Dam shortly before its collapse on June 5, 1976.
Aerial view of Teton Dam and reservoir around the time of the 1976 failure.
Growing breach in Teton Dam during the final hour before collapse.
Aerial view of the flooding downstream after the Teton Dam collapse.
The surviving remains of Teton Dam in Idaho, with the river passing through the unreconstructed breach.
Aftermath of the Teton Dam failure and downstream cleanup in Idaho.
Airborne radar view revealing structural elements of Camp Century beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet.
U.S. Army engineers constructing a steel-roofed trench at Camp Century on the Greenland Ice Sheet.
Camp Century trench deformation showing steel arches distorted inward by the surrounding firn and ice.
U.S. Army layout plan of Camp Century showing its underground corridors and facilities.
Camp Century scientists handling deep ice core material recovered from the Greenland Ice Sheet.
Camp Century map georeferenced to the 2017 radar-detected position beneath the moving Greenland Ice Sheet.

posts.title: They Thought They Had Ten Minutes

images.alt: Fire spreading among armed aircraft on the flight deck of USS Forrestal on July 29, 1967.
USS Forrestal sailors directing firefighting hoses across the burned flight deck during the 1967 fire.
Aerial view of the burned and damaged USS Forrestal flight deck after the 1967 fire.
USS Forrestal crewmen fighting and cooling wreckage on the flight deck after the 1967 fire.
U.S. Navy sailors training on a shipboard fire simulation at Farrier Firefighting School in Norfolk.
A Navy firefighting instructor beside the memorial to Gerald W. Farrier at the school that bears his name.
U.S. Navy destroyers wrecked along the California coast at Honda Point after the September 8, 1923 disaster.
USS Delphy and another wrecked destroyer at Honda Point after the 1923 disaster.
Early U.S. Navy radio station equipment in California, similar to the shore direction-finding infrastructure used in 1923.
Wrecked U.S. Navy destroyers at Honda Point after the 1923 disaster.
USS Chauncey and wrecked destroyers during rescue operations at Honda Point in 1923.
Aerial historical view of the Honda Point destroyer wreck field along the California coast.
